column11: Fu S, Huynh D, Poothakary M, 'A cross-sectional study using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program database to estimate the prevalence of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) in the United States', Hematol Transfus Cell Ther 2026;48(4):106507, doi:10.1016/j.htct.2026.106507 (PMID 42526166, PMC13449907): 5,746.7 prevalent MDS cases across a SEER population of 43,926,825, which is 13.08 per 100,000. Applied to the 340,110,988 US residents at 1 July 2024 (Census Bureau Vintage 2024, the denominator the book's other whole-population rows use): 13.08e-5 x 340,110,988 = 44,495
column12: the conservative end of a wide published range, taken on purpose and flagged. Cogle CR, 'Incidence and Burden of the Myelodysplastic Syndromes', Curr Hematol Malig Rep 2015;10(3):272-281, doi:10.1007/s11899-015-0269-y (PMC4553145) reports US prevalence estimates of 60,000 and 170,000 from German registry and NHANES extrapolations respectively, so the published spread is nearly threefold and this row sits below all of it. The reason to take the registry figure anyway is that it names a method and a denominator a reader can check, where the 60,000 to 170,000 pair are extrapolations from non-US data; the reason to distrust it is that cancer registries are known to under-capture MDS - the same Cogle review puts claims-based incidence in the over-65s at 75 to 162 per 100,000 against SEER's 20 - so this row is a floor rather than a central estimate

column11: the lower-risk share. NCT06847867 enrols IPSS-R very low, low or intermediate risk with an overall risk score of 3.5 or less and marrow blasts under 5%. In the development cohort for the IPSS-R itself - Greenberg PL et al., 'Revised international prognostic scoring system for myelodysplastic syndromes', Blood 2012;120(12):2454-2465, doi:10.1182/blood-2012-03-420489 (PMID 22740453, PMC4425443), 7,012 patients - the distribution across the five categories is Very Low 19% (1,313), Low 38% (2,646), Intermediate 20% (1,433), High 13% (898) and Very High 10% (722). Very Low plus Low is 57%
column12: conservative on purpose. The trial's score cut-off of 3.5 reaches into the Intermediate band, which spans scores above 3 to 4.5, so some Intermediate patients qualify and are not counted here. No published split of the Intermediate band at 3.5 was found. The trial's other requirements - anaemia, and one prior line of an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent or luspatercept that relapsed, failed or was not tolerated - are NOT in this share, because no US figure for that share could be sourced; they are carried in the penetration peak below

column11: a judgement carrying two things, with the arithmetic written out. The unsourced narrowing first: NCT06847867 enrols only lower-risk patients who are anaemic and have already relapsed on, failed or could not take an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent or luspatercept, and no US share for that state was sourced; roughly a third of lower-risk MDS is a reasonable reading of a population in which anaemia is the dominant cytopenia and ESAs are first line. The competitive share second: that population is the one Reblozyl (luspatercept) and Rytelo (imetelstat) are approved into, so momelotinib would be a third entrant into a small and recently crowded setting, and perhaps a fifth of the addressable patients at peak. 0.33 x 0.18 = 0.06

column11: a judgement that is mostly about diagnosis, not about competition, and the arithmetic is written out. The book's two VEXAS rows are measured on different things: 15,609 is UBA1 genotype prevalence from population exome screening, while 851 a year is diagnosed incidence from a UK haematological malignancy registry. Taken together they say that only a small fraction of carriers is ever identified and treated - at 851 new diagnoses a year against 15,609 carriers, roughly 5% of the pool enters clinical care in any year, and the registry-diagnosed stock is a small multiple of that. Against that denominator a first labelled treatment could reach a high share of the patients who are actually found, and the product of the two is small. No approved therapy exists for VEXAS, so competition is not the binding constraint; diagnosis is
